(Iwata H, et al. Breast Cancer Res Treat 2019;173:123–133; Ma SJ, et al. Breast Cancer Res Treat 2021;189:737–745; Hanson K, et al. J Clin Oncol 2021;39.15_suppl.591; Beitsch PD, et al. footnotes.vv: FDG-PET/CT is most beneficial and accurate for advanced disease (stage III) and invasive ductal (compared to lobular) histology, but may be useful in selected circumstances of earlier stage disease (stage IIA disease: cT1cN1, cT2cN0) such as: equivocal CT+ bone scan results; suspicion of undetected nodal and/or distant disease; and treatment response assessment. An FDG-PET/CT may be utilized as an adjunct to, or in lieu of, initial standard staging and may be performed simultaneously with diagnostic CT. Conversely, a bone scan or sodium fluoride PET/CT may not be needed if an upfront FDG-PET/CT clearly indicates consistent findings on both PET and CT components. footnotes.hhh: In clinical situations where a biopsy cannot safely be obtained but the clinical evidence
footnotes.iii: Tumor tissue or plasma-based circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) assays may be used and each of these have benefits and limitations for diagnosis and disease progression. Tissue- based assays have greater sensitivity for some alterations, but ctDNA may reflect tumor heterogeneity more accurately. If one specimen is negative for actionable biomarkers, testing on the alternative specimen can be considered.
footnotes.jjj: See NCCN Guidelines for Palliative Care and NCCN Guidelines for Supportive Care.
footnotes.kkk: Optimal management of oligometastatic stage IV breast cancers remains uncertain. Routine utilization of locoregional treatment of the primary tumor and ablative treatment for metastatic sites have not been demonstrated to improve survival outcomes in prospective trials, however, may reduce the risk of local progression and palliate symptoms. Compared with recurrent oligometastatic disease, patients with de novo oligometastatic cancer have better outcomes and therapeutic decisions should be individualized and discussed

footnotes.k: Special Considerations for Breast Cancer in Males (Sex Assigned at Birth) (BINV-J).
footnotes.ee: Although patients with cancers with 1%–100% ER IHC staining are considered ER-positive and eligible for endocrine therapies, there are more limited data on the subgroup of cancers with ER-low–positive (1%–10%) results. The ER-low–positive group is heterogeneous with reported biologic behavior often similar to ER-negative cancers; thus, individualized consideration of risks versus benefits of endocrine therapy and additional adjuvant therapies should be incorporated into decision-making. See Principles of Biomarker Testing (BINV-A).
footnotes.kkk: Optimal management of oligometastatic stage IV breast cancers remains uncertain. Routine utilization of locoregional treatment of the primary tumor and ablative treatment for metastatic sites have not been demonstrated to improve survival outcomes in prospective trials, however, may reduce the risk of local progression and palliate symptoms. Compared with recurrent oligometastatic disease, patients with de novo oligometastatic cancer have better outcomes and therapeutic decisions should be individualized and discussed in a multidisciplinary context. A large number of case series document long-term DFS for patients with de novo oligometastatic breast cancer who received multimodality therapy leading to NED. For de novo oligometastatic disease with favorable features (HER2+ or ER+, induced NED status after receipt of optimal multi-agent systemic regimens, limited sites of metastases, bone-only metastases, and young age/longevity), an aggressive multimodality approach involving locoregional therapy of the primary tumor, ablative treatment to all sites of metastases and "adjuvant-like" systemic therapy may offer improved long-term PFS and may be considered.
footnotes.ppp: Denosumab, zoledronic acid, or pamidronate (all with calcium and vitamin D supplementation) should be given (category 1) in addition to systemic therapy or endocrine therapy if bone metastasis is present, expected survival is ≥3 months, and renal function is adequate. Patients should undergo a dental examination with preventive dentistry prior to initiation of this therapy. The optimal schedule for zoledronic acid is every 12 weeks.
footnotes.qqq: Baseline assessment of bone density is recommended for patients receiving an aromatase inhibitor who are at risk of osteoporosis (eg, age >65, family history, chronic steroids).

footnotes.aa: According to WHO, carcinoma of no special type (NST) encompasses multiple patterns including medullary pattern, cancers with neuroendocrine expression, and other rare patterns.
footnotes.bb: There are rare subtypes of metaplastic carcinoma (low-grade adenosquamous and low-grade fibromatosis-like carcinoma) that are considered to have a favorable prognosis without adjuvant systemic therapies.
footnotes.cc: To be associated with favorable prognosis, the favorable histologic type should not be high grade, should be pure (>90% as classified on the surgical excision, not core biopsy alone), and should be HER2 negative. If atypical pathologic or clinical features are present, consider treating as ductal/NST. HISTOLOGY HR STATUS HER2 STATUS SYSTEMIC ADJUVANT TREATMENT
footnotes.dd: Correlation of histology, HR, and HER2 status should always be done with awareness of unusual/discordant or borderline results. See Principles of Biomarker Testing (BINV-A).

footnotes.k: Special Considerations for Breast Cancer in Males (Sex Assigned at Birth) (BINV-J).
footnotes.ee: Although patients with cancers with 1%–100% ER IHC staining are considered ER-positive and eligible for endocrine therapies, there are more limited data on the subgroup of cancers with ER-low–positive (1%–10%) results. The ER-low–positive group is heterogeneous with reported biologic behavior often similar to ER-negative cancers; thus, individualized consideration of risks versus benefits of endocrine therapy and additional adjuvant therapies should be incorporated into decision- making. See Principles of Biomarker Testing (BINV-A).
footnotes.gg: Adjuvant Endocrine ± CDK/4/6 Inhibitor Therapy and Principles of Adjuvant Endocrine Therapy (BINV-K).
footnotes.hh: mm ii Note: All recommendations are category 2A unless otherwise indicated.
footnotes.ii: The benefit of HER2-targeted therapy is uncertain in HER2-positive breast cancer with pT1a–b, N0 tumors, a population not studied in randomized trials. The decision
footnotes.jj: The absolute benefit of HER2-targeted systemic therapy is negligible in patients with HR-positive cancers and tumor size bordering on T1mic (<1 mm), and endocrine therapy remains a viable option for systemic treatment.
footnotes.kk: Consider adjuvant bisphosphonate therapy for risk reduction of distant metastasis for 3–5 years in postmenopausal patients (natural or induced) with high-risk node-negative or node-positive tumors.
footnotes.ll: Consider extended adjuvant neratinib following adjuvant trastuzumab-containing therapy for patients with HR-positive, HER2-positive disease with a perceived high risk of recurrence. The benefit or toxicities associated with extended neratinib in patients who have received pertuzumab or ado-trastuzumab emtansine is unknown.
footnotes.mm: Updated results from the adjuvant APHINITY trial in HER2-positive early breast cancer, with a median follow-up of 11.3 years, have confirmed the benefit of adding pertuzumab to trastuzumab plus chemotherapy in preventing recurrences.

nodes.mermaid_text:
graph LR
    N01["NCCN Guidelines Version 2.2026
Breast Cancer During Pregnancy"] --> N02["GENERAL CONSIDERATIONS FOR MANAGEMENT OF BREAST CANCER DURING PREGNANCY¹⁻³"]
    N02 --> N03["General Considerations
• Considerations and selection of optimal local therapy and systemic therapy are similar to that recommended in non–pregnancy-associated breast cancer.
• The selection and timing of chemotherapy, endocrine therapy, and RT are different for pregnancy-associated breast cancer compared to non–pregnancy-associated breast cancer.
• BCS during the first trimester of pregnancy can be considered in those who will require adjuvant chemotherapy and can have adjuvant RT delayed until after delivery.
• Chemotherapy should not be administered during the first trimester of pregnancy.
• RT should not be administered during any trimester of pregnancy.
• Coordination is recommended between the oncology and obstetrics teams to plan the optimal timing of systemic therapy administration during pregnancy.
• Considerations for postpartum chemotherapy are the same as for non–pregnancy-associated breast cancer."]
    N03 --> N04["Considerations for Systemic Therapy
• A fetal examination with ultrasound should be performed prior to systemic therapy administration to exclude pre-existing abnormalities.
• Standard-dose chemotherapy should be used based on actual weight.
• Anthracycline, cyclophosphamide, and taxanes appear to be safe during the second and third trimesters.
  ▸ Doxorubicin/cyclophosphamide every 3 weeks is preferred. Limited data suggest that dd AC with granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF) use during pregnancy appears to be safe.
  ▸ Weekly paclitaxel is preferred.
• Avoid chemotherapy after 35 weeks to allow maternal bone marrow to recover before the delivery.
• The following agents are contraindicated:
  ▸ Anti-HER2 therapies: trastuzumab, pertuzumab, ado-trastuzumab emtansine, fam-trastuzumab-deruxtecan-nxki, neratinib, lapatinib, tucatinib
  ▸ CDK4/6 inhibitors (there are no data on safety)
  ▸ Antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs): fam trastuzumab-deruxtecan-nxki, datopotamab deruxtecan-dlnk, sacituzumab govitecan-hziy
  ▸ Endocrine therapy: tamoxifen, aromatase inhibitor, gonadotropin-releasing hormone agonists/antagonists
  ▸ PARP inhibitors
  ▸ Immune checkpoint inhibitors"]
    N04 --> N05["Supportive Care Considerations
• Antiemetics: Ondansetron and metoclopramide are considered safe.
• NK1 inhibitors: Avoid using these, as data from human studies are lacking.
• Steroids:
  ▸ Methylprednisolone, prednisolone, or hydrocortisone are preferred.
  ▸ Avoid dexamethasone or betamethasone if possible.
• G-CSF: Use with caution. There are insufficient data to support G-CSF use, but it appears to be safe during pregnancy."]
    N05 --> N06["¹ Kesireddy M, Krishnamurthy J. Pregnancy-associated breast cancer: Key concepts for optimizing diagnosis and treatment. JCO Oncol Pract 2025;21:275-277.
² Poggio F, Tagliamento M, Pirrone C, et al. Update on the management of breast cancer during pregnancy. Cancers 2020;12:3616.
³ Boere I, Lok C, Poortmans P, et al. Breast cancer during pregnancy: epidemiology, phenotypes, presentation during pregnancy and therapeutic modalities. Best Pract Res Clin Obstet Gynaecol 2022;82:46-59."]
